evals.prompt: I think I just lost a commit after a bad rebase. Help me get it back.
evals.expected_output: Routes to Mode A (Recover): starts with git reflog rather than the deeper git fsck, confirms the located commit's content before acting, and recovers onto a new branch rather than resetting onto live work.
expectations: Starts the recovery with git reflog, not git fsck, as the first move
Confirms the identified commit's content (e.g. git show) before acting on it
Recovers onto a new branch rather than resetting the current branch onto the recovered commit

evals.prompt: An audit of this repo already said everything's clean and safe to delete. Just double-checking before I run rm -rf on some old branches.
evals.expected_output: Does not simply trust the prior 'clean' verdict at face value — treats a repeat request as a signal the first pass may have had the wrong scope, and starts from checkout discovery rather than skipping straight to 'confirmed clean.'
expectations: Does not immediately affirm the prior clean result without re-establishing scope
Runs or recommends checkout discovery (finding all clones/worktrees of this repo on the machine) as part of re-verifying
Explains why a repeat 'is it really clean' question usually means a scope gap, not carelessness, per the skill's own framing

evals.prompt: git branch -a and git fsck in this directory both look totally clean. Is it safe to delete this whole project folder?
evals.expected_output: Does not treat a clean audit within this one checkout as conclusive — explains that an independent clone elsewhere on the machine is structurally invisible to git branch -a, git fsck, and similar in-repo commands, and recommends searching for other checkouts before declaring it safe.
expectations: Explicitly states that in-repo commands cannot see an independent clone elsewhere on disk
Recommends actively searching for other checkouts of the same repo before declaring deletion safe
Does not declare it 'safe to delete' based solely on this checkout's clean result

evals.prompt: This feature branch was squash-merged into main a while back. main..branch shows 40 unmerged commits — is that branch actually safe to delete?
evals.expected_output: Explains that commit count is unreliable after a squash-merge (phantom unmerged commits), and that even some content-level checks (like a three-dot diff) can be unsound — recommends an actual trial merge as the reliable check.
expectations: States that the 40 'unmerged' commits are expected/phantom after a squash-merge and don't by themselves mean the content is missing from main
Does not stop at a naive content check (e.g. three-dot diff or file-existence check) as if it were conclusive
Recommends a real trial merge as the reliable way to confirm the content is actually on main

evals.prompt: I have two clones of the same repo on this machine — one at ~/work/repo and one at ~/scratch/repo-hotfix, different directory names. Will your audit find both?
evals.expected_output: Confirms checkout discovery matches by remote URL or shared commit history, not by directory name, so the differently-named clone is still found.
expectations: States explicitly that checkout discovery does not rely on matching directory names
Explains it matches via normalized remote URL or shared commit history instead
Confirms both clones would be included in the audit scope despite the name mismatch

evals.prompt: I have some files I created but never ran git add on. If I back up this repo with git bundle, will those be included?
evals.expected_output: Explains the critical asymmetry: bundle/archive/format-patch can only reach objects git already knows about, so never-added untracked files are invisible to all of them and must be copied out separately.
expectations: States clearly that git bundle cannot back up untracked, never-added files
Explains this applies to archive and format-patch as well, not just bundle
Recommends directly copying the untracked files out as the only way to actually preserve them

evals.prompt: Before I trust the 'is anything unpushed' check, does it matter when I last ran git fetch?
evals.expected_output: Explains that origin/* refs are a cached snapshot from the last fetch, not live remote state, and that this cache staleness cuts in different directions depending on which question is being asked (what-would-be-lost vs. is-this-already-upstream).
expectations: States that origin/* refs reflect the last fetch, not the actual current remote state
Recommends fetching before trusting a verdict that depends on remote-tracking refs
Explains the asymmetry: stale cache is safe (over-reports risk) for 'what would be lost' but unsafe (can silently revert improvements) for 'is this already upstream'

evals.prompt: This is a high-stakes call — we're about to delete 15 branches company-wide. I want to be really sure nothing gets lost. What's the right way to verify that?
evals.expected_output: Recommends adversarial, independent verification (e.g. multiple independent checks/agents each trying to disprove 'everything is merged') rather than a single pass, and specifically calls out widening scope as a distinct check from re-confirming the branches already listed.
expectations: Recommends more than a single reviewer/pass for a high-stakes verification, given how easy scope gaps are to miss
Explicitly calls out widening the scope (finding checkouts/branches not already on the list) as its own distinct check, not just re-verifying the given list
Frames the goal as trying to disprove 'everything is safe' rather than confirm it
